newsitem.title: LEBANON: Syria looks even to Iraq in search for allies.
newsitem.headline: Syria looks even to Iraq in search for allies.

text.p: Syrian President Hafez al-Assad is searching for allies, even long-time foe Iraq, to counter the increasing pressure he is feeling from the United States and Israel.

The veteran ruler has backed up his pronouncement that he sees no hope for Middle East peace under the current Israeli government with efforts to form a front opposed to the policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Assad has just given up getting anything out of Israel," said a Western military analyst. "Syria has every reason to feel threatened."
Syria is openly campaigning for a boycott of a Middle East economic summit in Qatar in November that would display Israeli acceptance in the region.
Washington has been just as blunt in pressing countries to attend, with the prestige of both Syria and the United States hinging out the outcome.

In recent months Assad has also promoted a rapprochement between his ally Iran and Arab states, which has eased the hostile rhetoric at least, and in June he moved suddenly to thaw decades of icy relations with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
A Syrian delegation that is now in Baghdad discussing border demarcation entered Iraq across a frontier that was opened only two months ago after 17 years of closure.

Bus travel between the two capitals began just over a week ago and advertisements for travel to Iraq are now appearing in a commercial weekly distributed by the government for free. The Syrian ministry of tourism has approved tours to Iraq.

The official Damascus press said a Syrian trade delegation would go to Baghdad on Friday to discuss sales under the U.N. oil-for-food deal that allowed Iraq to resume oil exports this year. Syria said last month it had already signed contracts for $20 million in food exports to Iraq.
These moves, however, underline Assad's weakness rather than his strength.

Syria in 1991 had abandonned its opposition to peace with Israel for the chance to regain the Golan Heights, the plateau dominating Israel's Galilee and the plain to Damascus. But any prospect of regaining the Golan, captured by Israel in 1967, seemed to disappear with the election of Netanyahu last year.

Adding to the threat felt by a country with increasingly outdated weapons, Syria has nervously watched growing military cooperation between well-armed Israel and the large army of Turkey. Syria feels squeezed between the two U.S. allies.
A renewal of Iraqi-Syrian ties, ending the hostility that has dominated relations constantly since the 1960s, makes strategic sense for both countries. They both need friends.
"If they have a common enemy -- and it looks like they do -- they probably will cooperate," said a Lebanese political analyst.
The road to Damascus now provides only the second way out of Iraq -- alongside U.S. ally Jordan -- since Iraq was cut off from the rest of the world for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

The shortest route for Iraqi oil to European markets would be via Syria, rather than the Turkish pipeline now used. Iraq this month raised the possibility of resuming shipments through Syria for the first time since 1982.

A senior Syrian oil ministry official said this week that he knew of no formal request, but added there was no technical obstacle to pushing the Iraqi oil through the 400 km (250 mile) pipeline to the Mediterranean coast at Banias. Syria has been using the pipeline to carry its own production.

But even if the U.N.'s oil-for-food agreement with Iraq was amended to allow exports via Syria, the history of the 500,000 barrel per day Kirkuk-Banias pipeline illustrates the obstacles to full Syrian-Iraqi cooperation.

The flow through the pipeline, originally built in 1952, was disrupted various times and was closed off by Iraq in 1976. It re-opened in 1979, only to close again in 1980 at the start of the Iran-Iraq war. Iraq resumed pumping in 1981 but saw Damascus shut the line a year later when Syria started receiving oil on concessionary terms from Iran.
Ingrained distrust is also a threat to Syrian hopes for a wider alliance.
Iraq and Iran, who fought a brutal eight-year war in the 1980s, have not been driven together even by the U.S. efforts to cripple both of them.

Saudi Arabia has backed Syria's opposition to the Qatar summit, but it distrusts Iran and fought Iraq in 1991. Egypt, which gets $2.1 billion in U.S. aid annually, has not echoed Assad's pessimism on the possibility of peace.

The Beirut-based Lebanese Centre for Policy Studies in its latest report predicted more diplomatic manoeuvring involving Assad in the coming months. But the results for the Middle East, it said, would likely be "fluid immobility".
